screens.title: Unit and Integration Testing with Jest & RTL
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn practical, repeatable techniques for verifying React Native components with Jest and React Native Testing Library. We start from setup and move through unit tests for simple, stateless components, integration tests for components that manage state or talk to services, and finally strategies to mock asynchronous dependencies like A P I calls. You will see how standard queries such as getByText and getByTestId let you assert what a user sees, how fireEvent simulates interactions, and why waitFor is essential when UI updates happen asynchronously. Along the way I’ll explain common mistakes—like testing implementation details instead of observable behavior—and show simple patterns to avoid them. For example, instead of asserting internal state, we assert visible text and side effects so tests stay stable as implementation evolves. By the end of this chapter you should be able to configure Jest with setupFilesAfterEnv, write a unit test for a presentational component, write an integration test that presses buttons and checks state changes, and mock a network call using jest. mock and jest. fn so tests remain fast and deterministic. What test will you write first to increase confidence in your app?

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Unit & Integration Testing with Jest & RTL

This module focuses on writing tests that assert what users see and do. We emphasize setup, common queries, event simulation, asynchronous assertions, and mocking external modules.

In this lesson
Configure Jest and RNTL, write unit and integration tests, and mock async dependencies.
Coming up
Examples for Greeting, Counter, UserList, and LoginButton with concrete tests and common pitfalls.
Explore Key Topics
Setup
Install RNTL and jest-native and configure setupFilesAfterEnv.
Queries & Events
Use getByText, getByTestId, fireEvent, and waitFor for assertions.
Mocking
Use jest.mock and jest.fn to replace API calls and control outcomes.
Visual Concept
Render
render(component) mounts a component for assertions.
Events
fireEvent simulates user interactions such as presses and text changes.
Async
waitFor waits for UI updates after promises or timeouts.
Mock
jest.mock replaces modules so tests are deterministic and fast.
This visual groups the main ideas you'll practice: mounting, interacting, waiting, and isolating dependencies.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will do four concrete things that make tests reliable and useful. First, you will set up Jest and React Native Testing Library so your project has the right matchers and a shared test environment. I will show how setupFilesAfterEnv imports jest-native matchers once so they are available in every test. Second, you will write unit tests for simple functional components that assert rendered text and testIDs rather than internal implementation. I will demonstrate a Greeting component test that checks visible text for stability. Third, you will write integration tests that simulate user interactions and state changes, using fireEvent to press buttons and assert the resulting UI. I’ll use a Counter example to make this concrete. Fourth, you will mock external modules and async operations so tests are fast and deterministic; we’ll use jest. mock and jest. fn to replace a fetchUsers service and show success and failure cases with waitFor. Each objective is practice-oriented so you can build tests that catch regressions without being brittle.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide ties each skill to a concrete task you will encounter. Configuring Jest means adding setupFilesAfterEnv so custom matchers like toBeOnTheScreen are available; this saves you from importing them in every test and reduces boilerplate. Writing unit tests for presentational components trains you to assert visible output based on props—this is faster and less brittle than checking internals. Integration tests help you verify interactions: when a user presses an Increment button the displayed count should update; you'll practice this with fireEvent and screen queries. Mocking external modules makes your tests deterministic: instead of hitting a real A P I you substitute a mock implementation that returns resolved or rejected promises to exercise success and error flows. Each objective is paired with a simple mnemonic: Setup → single shared file, Unit → props-in → visible-out, Integration → simulate events, Mocking → controlled responses. These mappings help you choose the right approach when you need a quick regression test or a deeper behavioral test of component interactions.

screens.title: Setting up Jest and React Native Testing Library
screens.narratorSegment: Setting up Jest and React Native Testing Library is the first practical step toward reliable tests. The minimal setup often includes adding @testing-library/react-native and @testing-library/jest-native to your devDependencies and creating a shared setup file referenced by Jest’s setupFilesAfterEnv option. That setup file typically imports jest-native/extend-expect so matchers such as toBeOnTheScreen and toHaveTextContent are globally available. Many projects created with the React Native CLI already include Jest, but adding RNTL and jest-native unlocks queries and matchers tailored to native components. A good setup also mocks any native modules your app relies on or provides a global wrapper for native features so tests run in Node without a device. Beware of a common misconception: you do not need to test implementation details. Configure the environment so you can write tests that assert observable behavior instead. As an example, a setup-tests. js file could import '@testing-library/jest-native/extend-expect' and set any global timers or mocks. This keeps individual test files focused and reduces boilerplate, helping your team write more expressive assertions. Setting up Jest and React Native Testing Library means use setupfilesafterenv to import jest-native matchers once and mock native dependencies so tests run reliably.. In practical terms, install packages and configure a shared test environment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Setup
Definition

Install and configure

A shared test setup imports matchers and establishes mocks so tests are consistent across files. This reduces repetition and ensures custom matchers are available globally.

Example setup file
// setup-tests.js
import '@testing-library/jest-native/extend-expect';
// global mocks for native modules can go here
Why it matters
Global setup removes boilerplate from individual tests and ensures consistent behavior across the suite.
Common mistake
Importing matchers in each file creates duplication and increases the chance of forgetting them in a new test.
Jest config snippet
{
  "jest": {
    "setupFilesAfterEnv": ["/setup-tests.js"]
  }
}
Check your understanding
  • Why import jest-native once instead of in each file?
  • Which native modules might need global mocks for tests to run?
Key Takeaway

Shared setup reduces boilerplate and gives you matchers and mocks available to every test file.

screens.title: Unit testing a functional component — Greeting
screens.narratorSegment: A unit test verifies a small unit of behavior in isolation. For presentational React Native components that receive props and render text, the most stable assertions check what users see. Consider a Greeting component that accepts a name prop and renders 'Hello, {name}!'. The test uses render to mount the component, screen. getByText to find the text, and a custom matcher toBeOnTheScreen to confirm it is present. Prefer getByText over getByTestId for visible content because tests that assert visible text reflect user-facing behavior and are less likely to be broken by refactors that don't change the UI. A common misconception is to assert internal implementation like useEffect calls or local state values; instead, assert the observable outcome. The included code block shows the component and three simple tests that render it with different props and check presence and text content. Running these tests validates that prop-driven rendering works and gives fast feedback when the component’s template changes. Unit testing a functional component — Greeting means assert observable output from props; prefer user-facing queries like getbytext for stable tests.. In practical terms, assert rendered text based on props using rntl queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Greeting Unit Test
Component
<!-- src/components/Greeting.tsx -->
import React from 'react';
import { Text, View } from 'react-native';

interface GreetingProps {
  name: string;
}

const Greeting: React.FC<GreetingProps> = ({ name }) => {
  return (
    <View>
      <Text testID='greeting-text'>Hello, {name}!</Text>
    </View>
  );
};

export default Greeting;
Test file
// src/components/__tests__/Greeting.test.tsx
import React from 'react';
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react-native';
import Greeting from '../Greeting';

describe('Greeting', () => {
  it('renders a personalized greeting', () => {
    render(<Greeting name='Alice' />);
    expect(screen.getByText('Hello, Alice!')).toBeOnTheScreen();
  });
});
Pro tip
Prefer queries that mimic how users find elements, such as getByText, for more meaningful tests.
Misconception
Testing implementation details like internal state increases brittleness and maintenance cost.
Key Takeaway

Unit tests should assert observable output for stability and clarity.

screens.title: Integration testing: Counter example
screens.narratorSegment: Integration tests verify how parts interact: UI elements, state, and handlers working together. The Counter component uses useState to track a numeric value and two buttons to increment and decrement it. An integration test mounts the component with render, uses screen. getByText or getByTestId to locate elements, calls fireEvent. press to simulate button taps, and then asserts the displayed count changed. This checks that button press handlers update state and the UI reflects that state. Integration tests are broader than unit tests because they exercise several pieces at once, but they still avoid external services. A common mistake is to assert implementation order or internal state directly; instead, assert that after pressing the Increment button the text reads Count: 1. In more complex components, chain multiple events and check the final visible result. Integration tests give you confidence that the UI responds correctly to user interactions and state changes without relying on external systems. Integration testing: Counter example means simulate user events and assert resulting ui changes to verify component interactions and state updates.. In practical terms, simulate events and assert state-driven ui updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Counter Integration
Process

Steps for an integration test

  1. Render the Counter component with render.
  2. Locate the count text and buttons using screen queries.
  3. Simulate presses with fireEvent.press.
  4. Assert the updated visible text matches the expected count.
Counter component
// src/components/Counter.tsx
import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { Button, Text, View } from 'react-native';

const Counter: React.FC = () => {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return (
    <View>
      <Text testID='count-value'>Count: {count}</Text>
      <Button title='Increment' onPress={() => setCount(count + 1)} />
      <Button title='Decrement' onPress={() => setCount(count - 1)} />
    </View>
  );
};

export default Counter;
Test snippet
// src/components/__tests__/Counter.test.tsx
import React from 'react';
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from '@testing-library/react-native';
import Counter from '../Counter';

describe('Counter', () => {
  it('increments the count when pressed', () => {
    render(<Counter />);
    const increment = screen.getByText('Increment');
    fireEvent.press(increment);
    expect(screen.getByTestId('count-value')).toHaveTextContent('Count: 1');
  });
});
Common mistake
Asserting internal variables rather than the visible UI increases brittleness.
Key Takeaway

Integration tests validate interactions and visible state changes, not internal implementation.

screens.title: Queries and Matchers: getByText vs getByTestId
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right query shapes how robust your tests are. getByText finds elements by their visible text and mirrors how a user identifies content, which makes tests meaningful and resilient to internal changes. getByTestId is useful when there's no visible text or when multiple elements contain similar text, but test IDs are implementation details and can be overused. For example, the Greeting component can be reliably asserted with getByText('Hello, Alice!'). The testID is handy for non-text elements like ActivityIndicator or complex list cells where accessible text is not present. Matchers round out the assertion: toBeOnTheScreen checks presence, toHaveTextContent verifies text content, and toBeDisabled asserts accessibility-enabled disabled state. A common misconception is that using getByTestId is always safer—overreliance on test IDs can hide regressions in what a real user would see. Prefer queries that reflect user experience, falling back to test IDs only when necessary. Queries and Matchers: getByText vs getByTestId means prefer user-centric queries like getbytext; use getbytestid sparingly for elements without visible text.. In practical terms, choose queries that reflect how users interact with the ui. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Queries & Matchers
When to use
getByText
Best for visible text assertions that reflect user experience.
getByTestId
Use when elements lack accessible text or in complex lists, sparingly.
Matchers
toBeOnTheScreen, toHaveTextContent, toBeDisabled are useful for clear assertions.
Example contrasts
Good
expect(screen.getByText('Hello, Alice!')).toBeOnTheScreen()
When to use testID
expect(screen.getByTestId('loading-spinner')).toBeOnTheScreen()
Misconception

Using test IDs everywhere makes tests pass even when the UI visible content is broken.

screens.title: Simulating user interactions with fireEvent
screens.narratorSegment: Simulating user interactions is essential for verifying how UI responds. React Native Testing Library provides fireEvent with helpers like press and changeText that let you simulate taps and text entry just like a real user. A typical pattern is: render the component, locate the interactive element with screen. getByText or getByTestId, call fireEvent. press or fireEvent. changeText, and then assert the resulting visible changes. For example, a LoginButton that calls an async onPress handler can be pressed via fireEvent. press and then you can wait for changes like a loading spinner or navigation side effect. One misconception is to rely on synchronous assertions immediately after fireEvent when the handler is async; if the handler triggers a state change after a promise resolves, use waitFor to wait for the UI update. Also be mindful that complex gestures require more setup—most common apps can be tested with press and changeText. Practice simulating sequences of events to validate the full user flow rather than single-click checks. Simulating user interactions with fireEvent means use fireevent to simulate user actions and combine with waitfor when handlers are asynchronous.. In practical terms, press, changetext, and other event simulations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › fireEvent
Common events
  • fireEvent.press(element) — simulate tap or press
  • fireEvent.changeText(element, 'value') — input text changes
  • fireEvent.scroll(list, { y: 100 }) — simulate scroll
Example
const button = screen.getByText('Login');
fireEvent.press(button);
await waitFor(() => expect(mockOnPress).toHaveBeenCalled());
Practical tips
Sequence events
Test realistic sequences: enter text, press, then assert resulting UI.
Async handlers
If handlers are async, use waitFor to observe state changes after the promise resolves.
Key Takeaway

Simulate the ways users interact and wait for async changes to assert the final UI state.

screens.title: Asserting asynchronous UI with waitFor
screens.narratorSegment: Asynchronous operations are common in React Native: network calls, timers, or other promises trigger state changes that re-render the UI. waitFor is a utility that repeatedly runs an assertion until it passes or a timeout is reached. Use waitFor when the effect you want to test happens after an async event. For example, a UserList component fetches users and renders a list; tests should assert that the loading indicator disappears and the user items appear after the mock fetch resolves. A common pitfall is asserting immediately after render—if the component updates later the assertion will fail. Another pitfall is not scoping waitFor narrowly; place the minimal assertion inside waitFor to reduce flakiness. Also be careful with long default timeouts; prefer to keep tests fast by controlling mocked promises and advancing timers if necessary. waitFor patterns keep tests robust and reflective of user-facing behavior when operations complete asynchronously. Asserting asynchronous UI with waitFor means use waitfor to poll assertions until ui stabilizes after asynchronous operations such as mocked api calls.. In practical terms, wait for ui updates triggered by promises or timers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › waitFor
When to use

Use waitFor when the UI changes after a promise resolves, a timeout runs, or an effect completes.

Example
// inside a test
await waitFor(() => {
  expect(screen.getByText('Leanne Graham')).toBeOnTheScreen();
});
Common mistake
Asserting too early, before promise resolution. Always wait for the expected UI change.
Practical checklist

  • Call render and trigger any actions that start the async flow.
  • Use waitFor to assert the final visible output.

waitFor helps tests observe UI updates after asynchronous work completes, keeping assertions reliable.

Mock pattern

jest.mock('../../services/api', () => ({
  fetchUsers: jest.fn(),
}));

// in a test
(apiService.fetchUsers as jest.Mock).mockResolvedValueOnce(mockUsers);
This replaces the real fetchUsers with a Jest mock you control for the duration of the test. Use mockResolvedValueOnce and mockRejectedValueOnce to vary responses per test.
Best practices

Component behavior
UserList fetches users on mount, shows an ActivityIndicator while loading, displays the list on success, and an error message on failure.
// src/components/UserList.tsx
import React, { useEffect, useState } from 'react';
import { Text, View, FlatList, ActivityIndicator } from 'react-native';
import { fetchUsers } from '../services/api';

const UserList: React.FC = () => {
  const [users, setUsers] = useState([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);
  useEffect(() => { /* fetchUsers and set state */ }, []);
  return loading ? <ActivityIndicator testID='loading-indicator' /> : error ? <Text testID='error-message'>{error}</Text> : <FlatList data={users} renderItem={({item})=><Text testID={`user-name-${item.id}`}>{item.name}</Text> /> />;
};
Test patterns
jest.mock('../../services/api', () => ({ fetchUsers: jest.fn() }));

it('renders users after successful fetch', async () => {
  (apiService.fetchUsers as jest.Mock).mockResolvedValueOnce(mockUsers);
  render(<UserList />);
  await waitFor(() => expect(screen.getByText('Leanne Graham')).toBeOnTheScreen());
});

Mocking API services and using waitFor covers loading, success, and error scenarios without network calls.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › LoginButton Tests
Component overview
// src/components/LoginButton.tsx
import React from 'react';
import { Pressable, Text, ActivityIndicator } from 'react-native';

const LoginButton = ({ onPress, title, isLoading=false }) => {
  const handlePress = async () => { if (!isLoading) await onPress(); };
  return (
    <Pressable testID='login-button' disabled={isLoading} onPress={handlePress}>
      {isLoading ? <ActivityIndicator testID='loading-spinner' /> : <Text>{title}</Text>}
    </Pressable>
  );
};
Test highlights
it('calls onPress when pressed', async () => {
  const mockOnPress = jest.fn().mockResolvedValueOnce(undefined);
  render(<LoginButton title='Login' onPress={mockOnPress} />);
  fireEvent.press(screen.getByTestId('login-button'));
  await waitFor(() => expect(mockOnPress).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1));
});
Edge case
Assert that isLoading disables the button and shows the spinner so users cannot double-submit.
Key Takeaway

Combine jest.fn, fireEvent, and waitFor to verify async handlers and conditional rendering.

screens.title: Clearing and resetting mocks between tests
screens.narratorSegment: Isolating tests requires that mocks and spies do not leak state between tests. Jest provides helpers like jest. clearAllMocks and jest. resetAllMocks to clear call history and reset mock implementations. A common pattern is to call jest. clearAllMocks in a beforeEach so each test starts with a clean slate. Without this, a mock's call count or previously mocked resolved values can affect subsequent tests, causing flakiness. For module mocks created with jest. mock, resetting implementations may be necessary when multiple tests need different behaviors from the same mock. The key idea is predictable, repeatable tests: each test should set up exactly the mocked return values it needs, run assertions, and not rely on previous test side effects. This discipline makes the suite easier to reason about and prevents subtle failures caused by stateful mocks. When you see intermittent failures, checking mock reset patterns is a good debugging step. Clearing and resetting mocks between tests means clear mocks in beforeeach so each test controls mock behavior and call history independently.. In practical terms, use beforeeach to avoid test pollution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Resetting mocks

Use jest.clearAllMocks in beforeEach to remove call history and ensure predictable behavior across tests.

describe('suite', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    jest.clearAllMocks();
  });

  it('test A', () => { /* mock and test */ });
  it('test B', () => { /* different mock and test */ });
});
Why
Avoid test pollution and flakiness by ensuring each test’s mock state is independent.
Pitfall
Not clearing mocks can cause subtle cross-test dependencies and intermittent failures.
Key Takeaway

Reset mocks between tests to keep suites reliable and easier to debug.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Experienced developers learn common testing mistakes and how to avoid them. One brittle pattern is asserting implementation details such as internal state or function call order; instead assert visible outcomes that matter to users. Another frequent error is failing to use waitFor for async updates—this causes tests to assert too early and yield false negatives. Over-mocking is also a hazard: mocking everything hides integration problems. The strategy is to mock external services but keep integration tests that exercise real code paths when appropriate. Forgetting to clear mocks between tests leads to cross-test pollution and flakiness; use jest. clearAllMocks or jest. resetAllMocks in beforeEach. Misusing test IDs instead of visible queries can allow broken UI to pass tests. The healthy balance is: test user-facing behavior, mock external dependencies, use waitFor for async updates, and reset mocks each test. This checklist will help you write tests that are fast, reliable, and maintainable. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn practical, repeatable techniques for verifying React Native components with Jest and React Native Testing Library. We start from setup and move through unit tests for simple, stateless components, integration tests for components that manage state or talk to services, and finally strategies to mock asynchronous dependencies like A P I calls. You will see how standard queries such as getByText and getByTestId let you assert what a user sees, how fireEvent simulates interactions, and why waitFor is essential when UI updates happen asynchronously. Along the way I’ll explain common mistakes—like testing implementation details instead of observable behavior—and show simple patterns to avoid them. For example, instead of asserting internal state, we assert visible text and side effects so tests stay stable as implementation evolves. By the end of this chapter you should be able to configure Jest with setupFilesAfterEnv, write a unit test for a presentational component, write an integration test that presses buttons and checks state changes, and mock a network call using jest. mock and jest. fn so tests remain fast and deterministic. What test will you write first to increase confidence in your app?

By the end of this chapter you will do four concrete things that make tests reliable and useful. First, you will set up Jest and React Native Testing Library so your project has the right matchers and a shared test environment. I will show how setupFilesAfterEnv imports jest-native matchers once so they are available in every test. Second, you will write unit tests for simple functional components that assert rendered text and testIDs rather than internal implementation. I will demonstrate a Greeting component test that checks visible text for stability. Third, you will write integration tests that simulate user interactions and state changes, using fireEvent to press buttons and assert the resulting UI. I’ll use a Counter example to make this concrete. Fourth, you will mock external modules and async operations so tests are fast and deterministic; we’ll use jest. mock and jest. fn to replace a fetchUsers service and show success and failure cases with waitFor. Each objective is practice-oriented so you can build tests that catch regressions without being brittle.

This second objectives slide ties each skill to a concrete task you will encounter. Configuring Jest means adding setupFilesAfterEnv so custom matchers like toBeOnTheScreen are available; this saves you from importing them in every test and reduces boilerplate. Writing unit tests for presentational components trains you to assert visible output based on props—this is faster and less brittle than checking internals. Integration tests help you verify interactions: when a user presses an Increment button the displayed count should update; you'll practice this with fireEvent and screen queries. Mocking external modules makes your tests deterministic: instead of hitting a real A P I you substitute a mock implementation that returns resolved or rejected promises to exercise success and error flows. Each objective is paired with a simple mnemonic: Setup → single shared file, Unit → props-in → visible-out, Integration → simulate events, Mocking → controlled responses. These mappings help you choose the right approach when you need a quick regression test or a deeper behavioral test of component interactions.

Setting up Jest and React Native Testing Library is the first practical step toward reliable tests. The minimal setup often includes adding @testing-library/react-native and @testing-library/jest-native to your devDependencies and creating a shared setup file referenced by Jest’s setupFilesAfterEnv option. That setup file typically imports jest-native/extend-expect so matchers such as toBeOnTheScreen and toHaveTextContent are globally available. Many projects created with the React Native CLI already include Jest, but adding RNTL and jest-native unlocks queries and matchers tailored to native components. A good setup also mocks any native modules your app relies on or provides a global wrapper for native features so tests run in Node without a device. Beware of a common misconception: you do not need to test implementation details. Configure the environment so you can write tests that assert observable behavior instead. As an example, a setup-tests. js file could import '@testing-library/jest-native/extend-expect' and set any global timers or mocks. This keeps individual test files focused and reduces boilerplate, helping your team write more expressive assertions. Setting up Jest and React Native Testing Library means use setupfilesafterenv to import jest-native matchers once and mock native dependencies so tests run reliably.. In practical terms, install packages and configure a shared test environment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A unit test verifies a small unit of behavior in isolation. For presentational React Native components that receive props and render text, the most stable assertions check what users see. Consider a Greeting component that accepts a name prop and renders 'Hello, {name}!'. The test uses render to mount the component, screen. getByText to find the text, and a custom matcher toBeOnTheScreen to confirm it is present. Prefer getByText over getByTestId for visible content because tests that assert visible text reflect user-facing behavior and are less likely to be broken by refactors that don't change the UI. A common misconception is to assert internal implementation like useEffect calls or local state values; instead, assert the observable outcome. The included code block shows the component and three simple tests that render it with different props and check presence and text content. Running these tests validates that prop-driven rendering works and gives fast feedback when the component’s template changes. Unit testing a functional component — Greeting means assert observable output from props; prefer user-facing queries like getbytext for stable tests..
